extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal education funds (K-12 and higher education) including Title IX coordinators, school administrators, investigators, decision-makers, and institutional legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements implementing Title IX grievance, recordkeeping, training-publication, and remedial obligations for institutions that receive Federal education funds. Covers what records to keep, retention periods, training publication, documentation requirements, and the Department's remedial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record retention period — seven years
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department extends the minimum record retention requirement from three years to seven years for records required under §106.45(b)(10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The seven-year period was selected for consistency with Clery Act recordkeeping and to address commenters' concerns that three years is inadequate (e.g., files destroyed before graduation). Recipients may retain records longer if desired or legally required. The Department declines to base the retention period on potential use in private litigation or on each student's enrollment duration; a standardized minimum is easier to meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of records to be maintained
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(10)(i)(A) requires recipients to maintain records of “each sexual harassment investigation.” Any record the recipient creates to investigate an allegation, regardless of later dismissal or resolution, must be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records include notes, reports, audio or audiovisual recordings or transcripts of hearings, investigative reports, written determinations, and any evidence directly related to the allegations. Recipients must preserve records even from truncated investigations that led to no adjudication. The date of a record's creation begins the seven-year retention period, and recipients may choose to retain records for longer, for example to ensure all records in a file are kept at least seven years from the date of the last record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties' access to evidence related to their case
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties to a formal complaint receive written notice of the allegations, the evidence directly related to the allegations, the investigative report, and the written determination, and have the right to inspect and review recordings or transcripts of live hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised the rule to remove a broad requirement to “make available to the complainant and respondent” to avoid disclosure of supportive measures. Instead, §106.45(b)(5)(vi) requires that the recipient provide both parties an equal opportunity to inspect and review any evidence obtained as part of the investigation that is directly related to the allegations raised in a formal complaint. Parties preparing for litigation or an OCR complaint are entitled to receive copies of those materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures confidentiality and access limits
rubrics_metrics.description: To protect confidentiality of supportive measures, the Department removed language that could have required making all records available to parties, and limited what must be shared to evidence and records directly related to allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change prevents disclosure to one party of the supportive measures or remedies provided to the other party while still ensuring parties have access to the materials necessary to respond to allegations. Recipients must balance access obligations with confidentiality of supportive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of training materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must publish on their websites the training materials referenced in §106.45(b)(1)(iii). If a recipient does not have a website, such training materials must be available for public inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published materials must be up to date and reflect the latest training provided to Title IX personnel. If training is provided by an outside consultant and materials are owned by the consultant, the recipient must secure permission to publish or create its own materials. Making training materials public is intended to improve transparency and integrity of the grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who must be trained and required training content
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(1)(iii) specifies that recipients must train Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and persons who facilitate informal resolutions on specific topics for specific purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule provides sufficient specificity for recipients to understand their obligations regarding retention and publication of materials used to conduct such training. Changes explicitly add persons who facilitate informal resolutions to the list of Title IX personnel whose training materials must be made available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation that response was not deliberately indifferent
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(10)(ii) requires a recipient to document its conclusion that its response to sexual harassment “was not deliberately indifferent” for each response required under §106.44(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must evaluate how they handled any report or formal complaint and document reasons why the response was not clearly unreasonable in light of known circumstances. If a recipient does not provide a complainant with supportive measures (e.g., complainant refuses them), the recipient must document the reasons why that decision was not deliberately indifferent. Example: when a Title IX Coordinator files a formal complaint against the complainant's wishes, the recipient should document why that decision was not clearly unreasonable. The Department allows later-added documentation or explanations but cautions that courts or agencies may scrutinize additions for fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ombudsperson records exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ombudspersons do not automatically fall under §106.45(b)(10); only records that an ombudsperson creates that the Department requires the recipient to maintain or publish are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(b)(10) identifies the types of records that must be kept, not categories of persons whose records are included. Unless an ombudsperson's records fall within those required types, they are not covered by this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department authority to require remedial action for regulatory violations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assistant Secretary may require recipients to remedy violations of Title IX implementing regulations even where the violation does not itself constitute sex discrimination, consistent with 20 U.S.C. 1682 (as reflected in revised §106.3(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects longstanding Department practice and statutory authority to promulgate rules to effectuate Title IX's purposes. The Department emphasizes remedial powers can be used for violations of the regulations as well as discrimination, and any party may request Department action against a noncompliant recipient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial action must be consistent with 20 U.S.C. 1682; approach to damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedial action the Department may require must be consistent with 20 U.S.C. 1682. The Department removed a proposed reference to “assessment of damages” from §106.3(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will not differentiate among potential remedies in the regulation itself; remedies may include equitable and injunctive actions and financial compensation to victims of discrimination or regulatory violations as necessary under the specific facts of a case. The rule avoids expressly prescribing monetary damages in regulation while acknowledging that some financial compensation may be ordered as equitable relief. Private lawsuits remain available for damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mandated Department-wide data collection or 'sealing' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to require the data collections requested by commenters concerning Title IX reports and formal complaints, and does not believe 'sealing' of records generally applies in most educational institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing in the final regulations precludes a recipient from collecting demographic data relating to its Title IX reports and formal complaints. The Department will not micromanage how recipients keep records beyond the specified requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients are not required to proactively send maintained records to parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department does not wish to burden recipients with a requirement to send the records it maintains under §106.45(b)(10) to the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, parties preparing for a lawsuit or OCR complaint are entitled to receive copies of the evidence directly related to the allegations raised in a formal complaint, the investigative report, and the written determination, and thus may obtain those materials through appropriate procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for standardized minimum retention rather than individualized retention
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to base retention around the length of time each student is enrolled and instead adopts a standardized minimum retention period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standardized expectation of the minimum time that Title IX records will be kept more easily allows recipients to meet the requirement than if timeframes were customized to each student's enrollment. The Department also believes seven years adequately covers most statutes of limitations that may apply to related causes of action.
